claim: A patient died as a result of septicaemia caused by a Klebsiella isolate, FK688, where the infection did not respond to treatment with carbapenems.
source: A patient died as a result of septicaemia caused by a Klebsiella isolate, FK688, where the infection did not respond to treatment with carbapenems (Bi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bi et al., 2017, which provides the source of this clinical case information.

claim: FK688 is a clinical isolate of Klebsiella quasipneumoniae.
source: Here, we reconstruct the genetic and evolutionary mechanisms of carbapenem resistance in a clinical isolate of Klebsiella quasipneumoniae.
evidence: The manuscript presents genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis that identifies FK688 as K. quasipneumoniae.

claim: The carbapenem-resistant strain FK688 carries no carbapenemase-encoding genes.
source: A combination of short- and long-read sequencing, machine learning, and genetic and enzymatic analyses established that this carbapenem-resistant strain carries no carbapenemase-encoding genes.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data, machine learning analysis using DeepBL, and functional testing of candidate genes.

claim: Two distinct genetic loci are necessary for FK688 to acquire carbapenem resistance.
source: Genetic reconstruction of the resistance phenotype confirmed that two distinct genetic loci are necessary in order for the strain to acquire carbapenem resistance.
evidence: This is confirmed through genetic reconstruction experiments and MIC testing of engineered strains.

claim: Both loci conferring carbapenem resistance confer a significant fitness cost.
source: Experimental evolution of the carbapenem-resistant strains in growth conditions without the antibiotic revealed that both loci confer a significant cost and are readily lost by de novo mutations resulting in the rapid evolution of a carbapenem-sensitive phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental evolution experiments and competitive fitness assays.

claim: Selection in the antibiotic ceftazidime can select for blaDHA-1, potentiating the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single mutation in ompK36.
source: Fitness assays in a range of drug concentrations show how selection in the antibiotic ceftazidime can select for one gene (blaDHA-1) potentiating the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single mutation in a second gene (ompK36).
evidence: This is supported by fitness assays conducted across a range of ceftazidime concentrations.

claim: A patient's treatment history might shape the evolution of antibiotic resistance.
source: These results show how a patient's treatment history might shape the evolution of antibiotic resistance and could explain the genetic basis of carbapenem-resistance found in many enteric-pathogens.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing how prior selection for blaDHA-1 facilitates subsequent carbapenem resistance evolution.

claim: Antibiotic resistance is driven by selection.
source: Antibiotic resistance is driven by selection, but the degree to which a bacterial strain's evolutionary history shapes the mechanism and strength of resistance remains an open question.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the evolution of antibiotic resistance.

claim: The source of antibiotic resistance can be the patient's own microbiome.
source: In the case of bacterial pathogens, there is mounting evidence that the source of antibiotic resistance can be the patient's own microbiome (Stracy et al., 2022) and that treatment history, as well as pathogen genotype, should be taken into account when designing a treatment plan.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stracy et al., 2022.

claim: Carbapenems are a class of β-lactam antibiotics typically reserved for high-risk, multidrug-resistant infections.
source: Carbapenems are a class of β-lactam antibiotics typically reserved for high-risk, multidrug-resistant infections (Doi, 2019; Meletis, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doi, 2019 and Meletis, 2016.

claim: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), especially various species of Klebsiella, have become a widespread problem in clinical settings around the globe.
source: Surveillance studies show that carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), especially various species of the pathogen Klebsiella, have become a widespread problem in clinical settings around the globe (Hansen, 2021; Hu et al., 2016; Logan and Weinstein, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple surveillance studies.

claim: There are two general mechanisms of carbapenem resistance.
source: There are two general mechanisms of carbapenem resistance.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of antibiotic resistance.

claim: The first mechanism of carbapenem resistance is the acquisition of a single gene encoding a carbapenemase enzyme that directly inactivates the antibiotic.
source: The first and readily diagnosable mechanism is the acquisition of a single gene encoding a carbapenemase enzyme that directly inactivates the antibiotic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carbapenem resistance mechanisms.

claim: The second mechanism of carbapenem resistance requires multiple genetic loci, often including an over expressed β-lactamase and/or an overexpressed efflux pump and/or an inactivated outer membrane protein.
source: The second mechanism requires multiple genetic loci, and bacterial strains in this category often have an over expressed β-lactamase and/or an overexpressed efflux pump and/or an inactivated outer membrane protein (Meletis, 2016; Codjoe and Donkor, 2017; Elshamy and Aboshanab, 2020), and potentially as yet unidentified loci as well.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: Most carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae are caused by carbapenemases.
source: Of these two mechanisms, most carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae that have been identified so far are caused by carbapenemases.
evidence: This is established knowledge from surveillance studies.

claim: Carbapenemases can be recognised by sequence analysis.
source: Like other β-lactamases, carbapenemases can be recognised by sequence analysis (Wang et al., 2021), and there are two structurally distinct classes of carbapenemases: the first is the metallo-β-lactamases a family of enzymes that contains a metal ion (usually zinc) coordinated in the active site, a classic example of which is NDM-1 (Khan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2021 and Khan et al., 2017.

claim: There are two structurally distinct classes of carbapenemases: metallo-β-lactamases and serine-based carbapenemases.
source: Like other β-lactamases, carbapenemases can be recognised by sequence analysis (Wang et al., 2021), and there are two structurally distinct classes of carbapenemases: the first is the metallo-β-lactamases a family of enzymes that contains a metal ion (usually zinc) coordinated in the active site, a classic example of which is NDM-1 (Khan et al., 2017). The second carbapenemase family does not coordinate a metal ion but instead relies on an active site serine to hydrolyse carbapenem drugs (Codjoe and Donkor, 2017; Nordmann and Poirel, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the structural classification of carbapenemases.

claim: The KPC-2 carbapenemase has become widespread and is found in many clinical investigations of CRE.
source: The KPC-2 carbapenemase has become widespread, found in many clinical investigations of CRE, and the gene encoding this enzyme - blaKPC-2 - is transferred readily by horizontal gene transfer via plasmids (Bowers et al., 2015; Hardiman et al., 2016; Kitchel et al., 2009; Petrella et al., 2008; Wyres et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Carbapenem resistance caused by the presence of a carbapenemase is readily diagnosed by whole genome sequencing or PCR-based genome tests.
source: Since this is a monogenic phenotype, carbapenem resistance caused by the presence of a carbapenemase is readily diagnosed by whole genome sequencing or even simple PCR-based genome tests.
evidence: This is inferred from the monogenic nature of carbapenemase-mediated resistance.

claim: Numerous CRE infections do not depend on the expression of carbapenemases.
source: It has recently become apparent that numerous CRE infections do not depend on the expression of carbapenemases, and there is mounting evidence that these non-carbapenemase CRE are widespread (Bouganim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bouganim et al., 2020.

claim: Non-carbapenemase CRE emerge because of reduced outer membrane permeability and/or increased drug efflux.
source: Based on the limited cases identified for non-carbapenemase CRE so far, it has been suggested that they emerge because of reduced outer membrane permeability and/or increased drug efflux (Logan and Weinstein, 2017; Goodman et al., 2016; Tamma et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: An extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) could provide sufficient activity against carbapenems to generate a CRE phenotype in some genetic backgrounds.
source: Other studies have suggested that, at least in some genetic backgrounds, an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) could provide sufficient activity against carbapenems as to generate a CRE phenotype (Codjoe and Donkor, 2017; Halat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Codjoe and Donkor, 2017 and Halat et al., 2016.

claim: Few studies have directly demonstrated the cause of non-carbapenemase CRE.
source: Despite this emerging knowledge, few studies have directly demonstrated the cause of non-carbapenemase CRE, and the evolutionary forces that shape the evolution of this trait have not been addressed.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The evolutionary forces that shape the evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE have not been addressed.
source: Despite this emerging knowledge, few studies have directly demonstrated the cause of non-carbapenemase CRE, and the evolutionary forces that shape the evolution of this trait have not been addressed.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in the literature.

claim: Understanding the details of evolutionary forces could provide a means to re-sensitise populations of bacteria to carbapenems.
source: Understanding the details of these evolutionary forces could provide a means to re-sensitise populations of bacteria to carbapenems.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the research.

claim: The complete genome sequence of Klebsiella FK688 was generated using a compilation of short- and long-read sequence data.
source: In this study, we present the complete genome sequence of Klebsiella FK688, using a compilation of short- and long-read sequence data (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing methods described and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FK688 carries a mega-plasmid (pNAR1).
source: We identify, and experimentally confirm the genetic basis of the non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype in FK688: carriage of a mega-plasmid (pNAR1) and an inactivating mutation in the chromosomal gene ompK36.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data showing the presence of a large plasmid.

claim: FK688 has an inactivating mutation in the chromosomal gene ompK36.
source: We identify, and experimentally confirm the genetic basis of the non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype in FK688: carriage of a mega-plasmid (pNAR1) and an inactivating mutation in the chromosomal gene ompK36.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data and structural analysis.

claim: Non-carbapenemase CRE strains are unfit and readily evolve to be drug-sensitive in the absence of carbapenem antibiotics.
source: We show that non-carbapenemase CRE strains are unfit and readily evolve to be drug-sensitive in the absence of carbapenem antibiotics.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental evolution experiments.

claim: The evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE strains may be contingent on their recent exposure to antibiotics that select for other β-lactamases.
source: The evolution of these low-fitness CRE strains may be contingent on their recent exposure to antibiotics that select for other β-lactamases which may explain the evolution of non-carbepenemase CRE.
evidence: This is inferred from fitness assays showing selection for blaDHA-1 in ceftazidime.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis placed FK688 within K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae.
source: Phylogenetic analysis placed FK688 within K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: FK688 carries a blaOKP-B-21 gene encoding a β-lactamase that confers resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins such as cefazolin.
source: Readily identifiable determinants of AMR on the FK688 chromosome are a blaOKP-B-21 gene encoding a β-lactamase that confers resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins such as cefazolin, as well as determinants for quinolone (oqxA, oqxB; Brisse et al., 2014; Mathers et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2019) and fosfomycin (fosA5) resistance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genome annotation and functional testing.

claim: FK688 carries determinants for quinolone resistance (oqxA, oqxB).
source: Readily identifiable determinants of AMR on the FK688 chromosome are a blaOKP-B-21 gene encoding a β-lactamase that confers resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins such as cefazolin, as well as determinants for quinolone (oqxA, oqxB; Brisse et al., 2014; Mathers et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2019) and fosfomycin (fosA5) resistance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genome annotation and citations.

claim: FK688 carries a determinant for fosfomycin resistance (fosA5).
source: Readily identifiable determinants of AMR on the FK688 chromosome are a blaOKP-B-21 gene encoding a β-lactamase that confers resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins such as cefazolin, as well as determinants for quinolone (oqxA, oqxB; Brisse et al., 2014; Mathers et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2019) and fosfomycin (fosA5) resistance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genome annotation.

claim: Eight candidate carbapenemases were identified in the FK688 genome sequence using DeepBL.
source: To identify any cryptic carbapenemases that may have escaped annotation, we made use of the machine learning predictor DeepBL (Wang et al., 2021). DeepBL identifies genes encoding β-lactamases of all types, including carbapenemases, and generated eight high-confidence predictions.
evidence: This is supported by the use of the DeepBL machine learning tool.

claim: Only OKP-B-21 and DHA-1 have β-lactamase activity that includes significant resistance to ceftazidime.
source: Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assays of E. coli expressing the DeepBL candidates showed that only OKP-B-21 and DHA-1 have β-lactamase activity that includes significant resistance to ceftazidime, a third-generation cephalosporin (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: This is supported by MIC assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Neither OKP-B-21 nor DHA-1 provided resistance to carbapenems.
source: However, neither OKP-B-21 nor DHA-1 - nor any of the other proteins tested - provided resistance to carbapenems.
evidence: This is supported by MIC assays of E. coli expressing these genes.

claim: The observed carbapenem-resistant phenotype for FK688 is not caused by a carbapenemase.
source: Taken together with the genome sequence analysis, these data support that the observed carbapenem-resistant phenotype for FK688 is not caused by a carbapenemase.
evidence: This is inferred from the genome analysis and functional testing showing no carbapenemase activity.

claim: K. pneumoniae has four genes encoding the major porins OmpK35, OmpK36, OmpK37, and OmpK38.
source: K. pneumoniae has four genes encoding the major porins OmpK35, OmpK36, OmpK37, and OmpK38 (Rocker et al., 2020), and the position and synteny of each gene in FK688 are conserved across K. quasipneumoniae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rocker et al., 2020 and genome analysis.

claim: FK688 has a 1.3 kb transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion within the 5' end of the ompK35 gene.
source: Inspection of the predicted protein sequences encoded by the four genes in FK688 revealed a 1.3 kb transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion within the 5' end of the ompK35 gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and a 48 bp in-frame deletion in ompK36 in FK688 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: FK688 has a 48 bp in-frame deletion in ompK36.
source: Inspection of the predicted protein sequences encoded by the four genes in FK688 revealed a 1.3 kb transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion within the 5' end of the ompK35 gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and a 48 bp in-frame deletion in ompK36 in FK688 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The deletion of 16 amino acids at the 3' end of the ompK36 gene in FK688 encompasses large portions of the β14 and β15 strands of the β-barrel structure.
source: The structure of OmpK36 (PDB 5O79) is known (Acosta-Gutiérrez et al., 2018), and the identified deletion of 16 amino acids at the 3' end of the ompK36 gene in FK688 encompasses large portions of the β14 and β15 strands of the β-barrel structure (Figure 2A and Figure 2B), explaining why the protein is not assembled into the outer membrane of FK688.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis using the known OmpK36 structure.

claim: The deletion in ompK36 explains why the protein is not assembled into the outer membrane of FK688.
source: The structure of OmpK36 (PDB 5O79) is known (Acosta-Gutiérrez et al., 2018), and the identified deletion of 16 amino acids at the 3' end of the ompK36 gene in FK688 encompasses large portions of the β14 and β15 strands of the β-barrel structure (Figure 2A and Figure 2B), explaining why the protein is not assembled into the outer membrane of FK688.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and immunoblotting data.

claim: The repaired gene encoding the porin OmpK36 restored carbapenem sensitivity.
source: Finally, measurements of carbapenem MIC determined that the repaired gene encoding the porin OmpK36 restored carbapenem sensitivity (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by MIC measurements shown in Table 2.

claim: After 11 passages, two replicates had completely lost resistance to the β-lactam antibiotic ceftazidime.
source: After 11 passages, two replicates had completely lost resistance to the β-lactam antibiotic ceftazidime.
evidence: This is supported by the mutation accumulation experiment.

claim: The first lineage lost a 17 kb region of pNAR1 that included the blaDHA-1 and qnrB4 antibiotic resistance genes flanked by the gene mobility elements tnpA-sul1 (pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1).
source: The first lineage lost a 17 kb region of pNAR1 that included the blaDHA-1 and qnrB4 antibiotic resistance genes flanked by the gene mobility elements tnpA-sul1 (pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1) while the second lineage lost the entire pNAR1 plasmid (pNAR1‾; Figure 3B, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing of evolved strains.

claim: The second lineage lost the entire pNAR1 plasmid (pNAR1‾).
source: The first lineage lost a 17 kb region of pNAR1 that included the blaDHA-1 and qnrB4 antibiotic resistance genes flanked by the gene mobility elements tnpA-sul1 (pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1) while the second lineage lost the entire pNAR1 plasmid (pNAR1‾; Figure 3B, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing of evolved strains.

claim: Loss of pNAR1, and specifically the tnpA-sul1 region of pNAR1, caused a loss of resistance to ceftazidime and carbapenem.
source: We assayed both the pNAR1‾ and pNAR1ΔblaDHA-1 strains for growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—source data 1) and antibiotic sensitivity (Table 2) and confirmed that loss of pNAR1, and specifically the tnpA-sul1 region of pNAR1, caused a loss of resistance to ceftazidime and carbapenem.
evidence: This is supported by MIC assays shown in Table 2.

claim: The acquisition of carbapenem-resistance in FK688 required the combination of the absence of porins and the β-lactamase DHA-1.
source: The results demonstrate that the acquisition of carbapenem-resistance in FK688 required the combination of (i) the absence of porins and (ii) the β-lactamase DHA-1 (Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic reconstruction experiments and MIC testing.

claim: The blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 alleles conferred a substantial fitness cost in growth media without antibiotic.
source: We found that the blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 alleles conferred a substantial fitness cost in growth media without antibiotic as compared to the other strains tested (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by competitive fitness assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The fitness defects of blaDHA-1 and ΔompK36 alleles are gradually reversed in the strains grown in the presence of increasing concentrations imipenem.
source: These assays showed that the fitness defects seen in the absence of imipenem (Figure 4B) are gradually reversed in the strains grown in the presence of increasing concentrations imipenem (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by fitness assays across a range of imipenem concentrations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A clinically relevant appearance of the CRE phenotype requires a combination of the presence of DHA-1 and the lack of a functional porin.
source: Thus, a clinically relevant appearance of the CRE phenotype requires a combination of the presence of DHA-1 and the lack of a functional porin.
evidence: This is inferred from the fitness and MIC data across different drug concentrations.

claim: Mutations that inactivate major porins restrict the permeability of the outer membrane.
source: Mutations that inactivate major porins restrict the permeability of the outer membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about porin function.

claim: The ΔompK36 pNAR1 (lineage A) populations evolved similar competitive fitness to the ompK36+ pNAR1 (lineage B) evolved populations, recovering the fitness cost of the ΔompK36 mutation.
source: The ΔompK36 pNAR1 (lineage A) populations evolved similar competitive fitness to the ompK36+ pNAR1 (lineage B) evolved populations, recovering the fitness cost of the ΔompK36 mutation (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by fitness assays of evolved populations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Each evolved strain independently sustained a deletion in pNAR1 that removed blaDHA-1.
source: To understand the molecular basis of these phenotypes, whole genome sequence data was analysed for four evolved strains: A2(o), A2(t), B3(o), and B3(t). Each, independently, sustained a deletion in pNAR1 that removed blaDHA-1.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing of evolved strains.

claim: The deletion of blaDHA-1 explains the increased carbapenem sensitivity of the ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1 lineages.
source: This explains the increased carbapenem sensitivity of the ΔompK36 pNAR1 and ompK36+ pNAR1 lineages as they had now lost one of the genes contributing to provide the phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic reconstruction experiments showing both genes are required.

claim: After 200 generations of evolution, samples displayed a mixture of opaque and translucent colony morphotypes.
source: After 200 generations of evolution, samples were plated on agar and were found to display a mixture of opaque and translucent colony morphotypes from each strain (Figure 5B and Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by colony morphology observations shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: Colony morphotype variation in Klebsiella spp. depends on the expression of type 1 fimbriae.
source: This feature has been seen before in Klebsiella spp. and depends on the expression of type 1 fimbriae (Matatov et al., 1999; Klemm, 1986; Struve et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the B3(o) isolate, a transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion had disrupted the downstream region of the fimE gene.
source: In the single B3(o) isolate recovered, a transposase gene (IS4 family) insertion had disrupted the downstream region of the fimE gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fimE gene was not disrupted in the A2 population that was capable of phase-switching.
source: The fimE gene was not disrupted in the A2 population that was capable of phase-switching (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A2(o) and B3(o) had more capsular polysaccharide than A2(t) and B3(t).
source: Consistent with these observations, an assay measuring glucuronic acid that reflects the presence of capsule showed that the A2(o) and B3(o) had more capsular polysaccharide than A2(t) and B3(t) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by glucuronic acid measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The ΔompK36 pNAR1 populations evolved increased sensitivity to imipenem, 64-fold for the A2(o) and A2(t) strains.
source: MIC analysis of the lineage A evolved strains showed that the ΔompK36 pNAR1 populations had evolved increased sensitivity to imipenem, 64-fold for the A2(o) and A2(t) strains, bringing them to the same MIC value as the B3(t) strain (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by MIC measurements shown in Table 3.

claim: The primary determinant of the reversion of the AMR phenotype is the observed loss of the blaDHA-1 gene from the megaplasmid pNAR1.
source: Our reconstruction experiments (Table 2) suggest that the primary determinant of this reversion of the AMR phenotype is the observed loss of the blaDHA-1 gene from the megaplasmid pNAR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the reconstruction experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: The evolution of imipenem resistance via multiple, low-fitness single-locus intermediates is puzzling because both the ΔompK36 strain and the blaDHA-1 positive strain each have a low fitness in growth media without antibiotic, as well as in growth media with imipenem.
source: The evolution of this trait is puzzling because both the ΔompK36 strain and the blaDHA-1 positive strain each have a low fitness in growth media without antibiotic, as well as in growth media with imipenem.
evidence: This is supported by the fitness assay data.

claim: The simultaneous acquisition of a new gene (blaDHA-1) and a spontaneous genetic variant (inactivating mutation in one or more major porins such as ompK36) is highly unlikely.
source: However, given that the two genes are not linked, the simultaneous acquisition of a new gene (blaDHA-1) and a spontaneous genetic variant (inactivating mutation in one or more major porins such as ompK36) is highly unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from basic principles of population genetics.

claim: The bacterial population may have first been subjected to environmental conditions that selected for the fixation of one of the alleles.
source: An alternative explanation is that the bacterial population may have first been subjected to environmental conditions that selected for the fixation of one of the alleles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the evolutionary trajectory.

claim: blaDHA-1 was selectively favoured in ceftazidime, even at concentrations approximately 100× below the clinical breakpoint of 16 µg/mL.
source: This showed that blaDHA-1 was selectively favoured, even at concentrations of ceftazidime approximately 100× below the clinical breakpoint of 16 µg/mL, despite the fact that carriage of the blaDHA-1 gene bears a substantial fitness cost (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by fitness assays in ceftazidime shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The OmpK36 inactivating mutation reduced fitness in ceftazidime.
source: In addition, we found that the OmpK36 inactivating mutation reduced fitness in ceftazidime, confirming that selection on ceftazidime can select for the blaDHA-1 gene, but not for the ompK36 mutation, which is required for imipenem resistance.
evidence: This is supported by fitness assays in ceftazidime.

claim: Selection on ceftazidime can select for the blaDHA-1 gene, but not for the ompK36 mutation.
source: In addition, we found that the OmpK36 inactivating mutation reduced fitness in ceftazidime, confirming that selection on ceftazidime can select for the blaDHA-1 gene, but not for the ompK36 mutation, which is required for imipenem resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the fitness assays showing differential effects of the two alleles in ceftazidime.

claim: Strains that carried only the ΔompK36 allele, or neither allele, were unable to evolve imipenem resistance.
source: We found that strains that carried only the ΔompK36 allele, or neither allele, were unable to evolve imipenem resistance (Figure 6B; "A" and "C").
evidence: This is supported by plating experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A K. quasipneumoniae strain with the pNAR1 plasmid (carrying the blaDHA-1 gene) would be readily able to evolve resistance.
source: However, a K. quasipneumoniae strain with the pNAR1 plasmid (carrying the blaDHA-1 gene) would be readily able to evolve resistance (Figure 6B; "B").
evidence: This is supported by plating experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In a scenario representing previous treatment of a patient with ceftazidime, the path A → B → D is most likely for the evolution of imipenem resistance.
source: Thus, in a scenario representing previous treatment of a patient with ceftazidime, given the low fitness benefit conferred by the loss of function mutation in ompK36 in growth media supplemented with imipenem, the path A → B → D is most likely.
evidence: This is inferred from the fitness data and evolutionary potential experiments.

claim: This study presented the first physical genetic map of a K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae genome.
source: This study presented the first physical genetic map of a K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae genome.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the genome assembly.

claim: Carbapenem sensitivity was restored with ease in the absence of drug selection.
source: A major finding of the study is the ease with which carbapenem sensitivity was restored in the absence of drug selection.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental evolution data.

claim: An ill-chosen drug treatment, for example with ceftazidime, can prime a population of K. quasipneumoniae to rapidly evolve a CRE phenotype.
source: A further major finding is the means by which an ill-chosen drug treatment, for example with ceftazidime, can prime a population of K. quasipneumoniae to rapidly evolve a CRE phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the fitness assays showing selection for blaDHA-1 in ceftazidime.

claim: KPC-2 carbapenemases are widespread in Klebsiella spp. including K. quasipneumoniae.
source: Genomics-based surveillance has shown that KPC-2 carbapenemases are widespread in Klebsiella spp. including K. quasipneumoniae (Mathers et al., 2019; Octavia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to surveillance studies.

claim: β-lactamases encoded by chromosomal genes are common amongst Klebsiella species.
source: β-lactamases encoded by chromosomal genes are common amongst these species of Klebsiella: blaSHV is found in K. pneumoniae, blaOKP-A in K. quasipneumoniae subsp. quasipneumoniae and blaOKP-B in K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae (Rodrigues et al., 2019; Long et al., 2017; Fevre et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: FK688 carries a chromosomally located blaOKP-B.
source: Consistent with this, FK688 carries a chromosomally located blaOKP-B.
evidence: This is supported by genome annotation.

claim: FK688 carries the β-lactamase blaDHA-1 on the megaplasmid pNAR1.
source: In addition, FK688 also carries the β-lactamase blaDHA-1 on the megaplasmid pNAR1.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing and annotation.

claim: There have been no reports on drug efflux pumps in K. quasipneumoniae.
source: There have been no reports on drug efflux pumps in K. quasipneumoniae, but in some strains of K. pneumoniae, drug-resistance phenotypes have been suggested to include epistatic contributions from genes encoding efflux pumps (Nicolas-Chanoine et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: In FK688, the efflux pumps did not contribute to carbapenem resistance.
source: In FK688, the efflux pumps did not contribute to carbapenem resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic reconstruction experiments showing only blaDHA-1 and ompK36 are required.

claim: The CRE phenotype in FK688 depends on epistasis between blaDHA-1 and ompK36.
source: Instead, we found that the CRE phenotype in FK688 depends on epistasis between blaDHA-1 and ompK36.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic reconstruction and fitness experiments.

claim: Both the carriage of blaDHA-1 and the defect in ompK36 have measurable fitness cost to the strain.
source: Both the carriage of blaDHA-1 and the defect in ompK36 have measurable fitness cost to the strain.
evidence: This is supported by competitive fitness assays.

claim: After multiple rounds of plating in the absence of drug-selection, the loss of a segment (tnpA-sul1) of pNAR1 that carries blaDHA-1 was observed.
source: After multiple rounds of plating in the absence of drug-selection, we observed the loss of a segment (tnpA-sul1) of pNAR1 that carries blaDHA-1, that is, selection against the β-lactamase.
evidence: This is supported by the mutation accumulation experiment.

claim: In the absence of β-lactam, the CRE phenotype is reversed to carbapenem-sensitivity.
source: Thus, in the absence of β-lactam, the CRE phenotype is reversed to carbapenem-sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental evolution and MIC data.

claim: The presence of plasmids encoding DHA-1 is geographically wide-spread.
source: It is not clear from current literature how widespread the non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype is, but several points are worthy of note: (i) the presence of plasmids encoding DHA-1 is geographically wide-spread (Hennequin et al., 2012), (ii) the presence of ompK35 and/or ompK36 mutations is prevalent in the various species of Klebsiella (Rocker et al., 2020), and (iii) a recent case study showed a single hospital had collected 87 isolates of CRE Klebsiella with 55% of them being a non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype (Tamma et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hennequin et al., 2012.

claim: The presence of ompK35 and/or ompK36 mutations is prevalent in the various species of Klebsiella.
source: It is not clear from current literature how widespread the non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype is, but several points are worthy of note: (i) the presence of plasmids encoding DHA-1 is geographically wide-spread (Hennequin et al., 2012), (ii) the presence of ompK35 and/or ompK36 mutations is prevalent in the various species of Klebsiella (Rocker et al., 2020), and (iii) a recent case study showed a single hospital had collected 87 isolates of CRE Klebsiella with 55% of them being a non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype (Tamma et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rocker et al., 2020.

claim: A recent case study showed a single hospital had collected 87 isolates of CRE Klebsiella with 55% of them being a non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype.
source: It is not clear from current literature how widespread the non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype is, but several points are worthy of note: (i) the presence of plasmids encoding DHA-1 is geographically wide-spread (Hennequin et al., 2012), (ii) the presence of ompK35 and/or ompK36 mutations is prevalent in the various species of Klebsiella (Rocker et al., 2020), and (iii) a recent case study showed a single hospital had collected 87 isolates of CRE Klebsiella with 55% of them being a non-carbapenemase CRE phenotype (Tamma et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tamma et al., 2017a.

claim: A personalised approach to antibiotic dosing has been urged to obtain the best outcome from the limited treatment options effective against CRE.
source: To obtain the best outcome from the limited treatment options effective against CRE, a personalised approach to antibiotic dosing has been urged (Doi, 2019; Doi and Paterson, 2015; Reyes and Nicolau, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical recommendations.

claim: All of the currently available tests for CRE aim to identify specific carbapenemases.
source: All of the currently available tests for CRE aim to identify specific carbapenemases: the Carba NP test detects OXA-48 type carbapenemases, the modified Hodge test identifies metallo-β-lactamases (Kuchibiro et al., 2018), and the newer more sophisticated gene-specific tests also have limitations (Tamma et al., 2017b; Powell et al., 2017; Revez et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2019; Meunier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple diagnostic studies.

claim: In some environments perhaps half of all CRE cases could be caused by strains that do not encode a carbapenemase.
source: The finding that in some environments perhaps half of all CRE cases could be caused by strains that do not encode a carbapenemase (Tamma et al., 2017a), and our finding that DHA-1 expression can - through epistasis with porin mutations - deliver a CRE phenotype adds a further degree of difficulty to diagnosis of CRE.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tamma et al., 2017a.

claim: Combination therapy using an ESBL inhibitor such as avibactam or tazobactam could be a good option for non-carbapenemase CRE.
source: First, combination therapy using an ESBL inhibitor such as avibactam or tazobactam could be a good option for this type of CRE (Yahav et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yahav et al., 2020 and inferred from the mechanism of resistance.

claim: The use of ceftolozane-tazobactam combination therapy is suggested as an alternative to carbapenems in treatment of some CRE infections.
source: For example, the use of ceftolozane-tazobactam combination therapy is suggested as an alternative to carbapenems in treatment of some CRE infections (Giacobbe et al., 2018), and a cohort study of 391 patients with ceftriaxone-resistant infections showed piperacillin-tazobactam combination therapy compared favourably with carbapenem treatment (Harris et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Phage therapy being used to treat CRE should avoid the use of phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor.
source: Second, our study cautions that moves towards phage therapy being used to treat CRE should avoid the use of phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor (Rosas and Lithgow, 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that porin loss confers carbapenem resistance and cited work on phage resistance.

claim: Phages that use OmpK35 or OmpK36 as their receptor would place selective pressure on the Klebsiella strain to become porin-defective since mutations to inactivate the receptor is a prime cause of phage-resistance.
source: These phages would place selective pressure on the Klebsiella strain to become porin-defective since mutations to inactivate the receptor is a prime cause of phage-resistance (Gordillo Altamirano et al., 2021; Gordillo Altamirano and Barr, 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of phage resistance and supported by citations.

claim: The evolutionary history of a pathogenic strain can predispose for an AMR phenotype to evolve via specific genetic routes.
source: Finally, this study shows how the evolutionary history of a pathogenic strain can predispose for an AMR phenotype to evolve via specific genetic routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing how prior selection shapes subsequent evolution.

claim: If antibiotic resistance genes are not supplied via horizontal gene transfer, then antibiotic resistance must evolve by the de novo mutation of a gene already present in the genome.
source: If antibiotic resistance genes are not supplied via horizontal gene transfer, then antibiotic resistance must evolve by the de novo mutation of a gene already present in the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolution of antibiotic resistance.

claim: The spontaneous acquisition of multiple genetic variants (for example, ΔompK36 and blaDHA-1) is much less likely than the acquisition of a single new gene (KPC-2 carbapenemase).
source: Since the spontaneous acquisition of multiple genetic variants (for example,ΔompK36 and blaDHA-1) is much less likely than the acquisition of a single new gene (KPC-2 carbapenemase), the evolution of non-carbapenem resistance via two loci seemed unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from basic principles of population genetics.

claim: If a strain already carries the blaDHA-1 gene then the spontaneous evolution of a loss-of-function mutation in ompK36 is more likely than the spontaneous acquisition of a carbapenemase gene.
source: However, if a strain already carries the blaDHA-1 gene then the spontaneous evolution of a loss-of-function mutation in an extant chromosomal gene - ompK36 - is more likely than the spontaneous acquisition of a carbapenemase gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the relative probabilities of different mutational events.

claim: Exposure to ceftazidime, or any antibiotic that selects for the blaDHA-1 gene, would potentiate the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single loss-of-function mutation in major porins.
source: Exposure to ceftazidime, or any antibiotic that selects for the blaDHA-1 gene, would therefore potentiate the evolution of carbapenem resistance by a single loss-of-function mutation in major porins.
evidence: This is inferred from the fitness assays and evolutionary potential experiments.

claim: An individual's treatment history might shape the evolution of AMR and should be taken into consideration to explain the evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE.
source: These results show how an individual's treatment history might shape the evolution of AMR and should be taken into consideration in order to explain the evolution of non-carbapenemase CRE.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing how prior antibiotic exposure shapes subsequent resistance evolution.

claim: The FK688 genome assembly revealed a circular chromosome (5,211,811 bp) and a novel circular megaplasmid (pNAR; 1,257,585 bp).
source: The genome assembly revealed a circular chromosome (5,211,811 bp) and a novel circular megaplasmid (pNAR; 1,257,585 bp).
evidence: This is supported by the genome sequencing and assembly data.

claim: The pNAR1 plasmid carried many antibiotic resistance genes corresponding to the known resistance profile.
source: This plasmid carried many antibiotic resistance genes corresponding to the known resistance profile (Bi et al., 2017), as well as genes encoding efflux pumps and other transporters (Figure 1—source data 3, Figure 1-source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by genome annotation and comparison with the known resistance profile.

claim: FK688 encodes numerous ABC-type efflux systems with annotations for metal ion ligands (copper, silver, and mercury).
source: FK688 encodes numerous ABC-type efflux systems with annotations for these efflux pumps suggestive of metal ion ligands (copper, silver, and mercury), but the ligand specificity of efflux pumps can be broader or different to that denoted by annotation (Mata et al., 2000; Flach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by genome annotation and citations about efflux pump specificity.

claim: OmpA does not form a sizeable channel in the outer membrane.
source: However, (i) OmpA does not form a sizeable channel in the outer membrane (Ortiz-Suarez et al., 2016), and (ii) while the porin PhoE does form a channel (Rocker et al., 2020), it is not conducive to permitting imipenem entry into Klebsiella (Rocker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ortiz-Suarez et al., 2016.

claim: While the porin PhoE does form a channel, it is not conducive to permitting imipenem entry into Klebsiella.
source: However, (i) OmpA does not form a sizeable channel in the outer membrane (Ortiz-Suarez et al., 2016), and (ii) while the porin PhoE does form a channel (Rocker et al., 2020), it is not conducive to permitting imipenem entry into Klebsiella (Rocker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rocker et al., 2020.

claim: A single SNP that was fixed in the A2 population was in the cadBA operon that generates cadaverine.
source: A single SNP that was fixed in the A2 population was in the cadBA operon that generates cadaverine (Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing of evolved strains.

claim: CadC is a positive activator of the cadBA operon.
source: CadC is a positive activator of the cadBA operon (DelaVega and Delcour, 1995), and this activation of cadBA is known to close porins in general and block β-lactam influx (Dela Vega and Delcour, 1996; Iyer and Delcour, 1997; Samartzidou et al., 2003), with point mutations in the CadC protein sufficient to inhibit the cadBA operon (Schlundt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on the cadBA operon.

claim: Activation of cadBA is known to close porins in general and block β-lactam influx.
source: CadC is a positive activator of the cadBA operon (DelaVega and Delcour, 1995), and this activation of cadBA is known to close porins in general and block β-lactam influx (Dela Vega and Delcour, 1996; Iyer and Delcour, 1997; Samartzidou et al., 2003), with point mutations in the CadC protein sufficient to inhibit the cadBA operon (Schlundt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.
